events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Sam proposes Sam, Leo. As Merlin I know Arjun and Isha are Evil, so I am proposing Sam and Leo, keeping both Evil players off the mission 1 team. Leo is the best untested choice, and I will include myself as a known-good member.

Sam’s proposal rests on an extraordinary public Merlin claim. I know my own loyalty, so his assertion that I am Evil is false. Either Sam is Evil and using a bold bluff to discredit me, or he is Good and making a reckless mission-1 declaration that gives Evil an easy target. In either case, we should not reward an unverified claim by sending his hand-picked team. Leo has not spoken, and Sam’s framing of Isha and me before any mission evidence is convenient. I will vote against this team and urge others to scrutinize the claim rather than treat it as settled.

Arjun, you asked for scrutiny, which is fair, but you have not named a concrete objection to this two-player team. I am Good, and Sam and Leo contain no player I know to be Evil. Mission 1 is a small test. Rejecting this team gives us no information, while approving it lets us see how Leo plays. If you believe my role claim is false, what specific evidence would make you approve a team that includes me? Please answer that directly.

Sam, I will answer your direct question. You asked what specific evidence would make me approve a team including you. The answer is evidence, not a pre-mission role declaration. Your proposal is Sam and Leo, and your justification is that you are Merlin and therefore know Isha and me to be Evil. I know my own loyalty, so that accusation against me is false. That does not prove you are Evil; it could mean you are Good and reckless, or Evil and bluffing. Either way, a public Merlin claim before any mission result is not a reason to trust your hand-picked team. Leo has not spoken, so including Leo is an untested choice, not a verified one. Mission 1 is small, but approving Sam and Leo rewards an unverified claim and gives no independent check on the leader. If you are Good, you have made yourself a target and asked us to accept your word as proof. I will not treat self-certification as evidence. I would need mission outcomes, a consistent explanation, or corroboration from another player before I support a team built on that claim. For now I oppose Sam and Leo.

Arjun, you asked what evidence would earn your approval, and you have not named a concrete flaw in Sam and Leo beyond my role claim. The team has two players and is a mission-1 test, so rejecting it gives us no information about anyone. I know my own role and the two Evil players I have identified, and I am not asking anyone to take that on faith alone. Leo, you have not spoken yet. Do you accept being on this two-player mission-1 team, and what would you need to know before you vote?

Sam, you yielded to me, so I will respond directly. I accept being on this mission-1 team. I am Good, and I have no reason to reject a team that includes me. That said, Sam's public Merlin claim is a big deal, and I want to weigh it carefully rather than dismiss it out of hand. Arjun's objection is reasonable on its face — a pre-mission role declaration is not proof. But Arjun, your counter has been entirely defensive. You have not proposed what a better mission-1 team would look like or who you would include. If you think Sam is Evil, name who you trust instead. Felix and Isha, I have not heard from either of you. Felix, what is your read on Sam's claim? Do you find it credible, or do you think it is a bluff?

Sam, your mission-1 proposal rests entirely on one unverified assertion, and you have repeated it three times without adding evidence. That does not make it true; it makes it the only thing we have to judge you by. A leader who stakes the first team on self-certification deserves exactly the scrutiny Arjun has given you, and he has not received an answer to it.

Let me be clear that Arjun's objection has been methodological, not personal. He asked what evidence would satisfy him and was given more assertion. That is a fair criticism of process. Leo, you accepted the team, and that is fine, but your acceptance leaned partly on Sam's word, which is circular for a mission whose only product is evidence.

So I want a concrete alternative on the table rather than a bare rejection. Sam and Leo is the claim-maker plus one player who has never been tested against him. The two-player team I would rather see is Leo and Arjun, or Sam and Arjun. Either way it includes a player whose position was formed independently of Sam's declaration, so the mission produces information about the players instead of about Sam's confidence. If Sam's claim is genuine, he loses nothing by defending himself alongside Arjun; if it is a bluff, having Arjun on the team costs the bluff very little and gains us real information.

Arjun, you have challenged the claim twice on procedural grounds without ever naming a team you would actually support, and that is why we still have nothing to vote on. If Sam's claim were false, which two-player team would you consider more trustworthy than Sam and Leo, and would you accept a place on it yourself? Answer that directly so the leader has a concrete revision to consider.

I will vote against Sam and Leo as it stands unless it is revised to include a player other than the one making the claim.

Isha, you asked directly, so I will answer concretely. If Sam’s Merlin claim is false—or even if it is true but unproven—the team I would consider more trustworthy than Sam and Leo is Leo and me. I know my own loyalty. Leo has at least engaged with the proposal and accepted a mission-1 test; pairing him with a player Sam has accused gives the table an independent check instead of a team built around Sam’s self-certification. I would accept a place on that team. That is not an endorsement of Sam’s accusation against me; it is false. It is also not an endorsement of Sam’s claim. The problem with Sam and Leo is not that Leo is untested—it is that the leader is asking us to validate a pre-mission role declaration by sending his hand-picked pair. A Leo-and-Arjun team would produce information about two players without making the first mission a referendum on Sam’s word. I will vote against Sam and Leo as proposed unless it is revised to remove that circularity.

I oppose Sam and Leo as proposed, and my reason has not changed: this team cannot produce information. It is the claim-maker plus one player who has never tested himself against anyone, and its only shared premise is Sam's word. If Sam's declaration is genuine, then Sam and Leo are two of the safest members on the table, and this mission reveals nothing about anyone else. If the declaration is false, then approving it ratifies a bluff and hands the first mission to whoever the bluer wanted on it. Either way the table learns nothing about loyalty, and we spend a mission slot to find out. A rejection costs us only a second proposal; Arjun has already put a concrete alternative on the table, a team of Leo and Arjun, which pairs two players whose positions were formed independently of Sam's claim and gives us a real signal about two people instead of about one man's confidence. Arjun has answered every direct question with specifics, named a team, and accepted a place on it; Sam has answered none of them with anything beyond repetition of the same assertion, three times over. That asymmetry is what should decide the vote, not the volume of the claim. I also note for the record that I have never endorsed Sam's accusation against Arjun. I find it unproven, and I have said so. What I am objecting to is the procedure: a leader who stakes the first team on self-certification, and then answers scrutiny by repeating the certification, has not earned the table's mission-one pair. I would rather this team go down and let a fresh leader be tested by a fresh proposal, because a leader who survives scrutiny is worth more to us than a leader who only survives because nobody asked a second question. Felix, you are the one voice I have not heard from, and your silence is the pivot on which this vote turns. Do you think Sam and Leo is worth approving on the strength of a single unverified claim, and are you willing to vote against it so that a second, independently formed proposal can be put to us? Answer that directly and I will take your read as binding on my own vote.

Isha, you asked for my read directly, so here it is. First, I decline the offer to have my vote treated as binding on yours. Nobody at this table should hand another player that much leverage after one conversation, and I won't accept that arrangement in either direction.

My read on Sam and Leo: I lean toward approving it, and here is why. The Merlin claim is unverified, that is true. But this team is actually a clean experiment. If Sam is Good and genuinely Merlin, Sam and Leo are two of the safest members available and mission one succeeds. If Sam is Evil and bluffing, he has placed himself on a two-player mission where a single Fail card points straight at the claim-maker — the result convicts him at the cost of one mission slot. Either branch produces real information, which is more than most mission-one proposals can promise.

Now contrast the alternative on the table. Arjun named Leo and Arjun. Isha endorsed Leo and Arjun, or Sam and Arjun. Notice the pattern: both accused players have converged on alternatives that always include one of the accused. If Sam's accusation is correct, those proposals put an Evil player on the very mission meant to test the accusation — the one outcome that guarantees no information, because an Evil member simply plays Success and launders their credibility for later rounds. If Sam's accusation is wrong, then Arjun and Isha are Good and their preference is honest. But their arguments do not distinguish those cases for us; approving a team containing a possibly-Evil accused player is what actually distinguishes them, and it distinguishes them badly for Evil.

I also want to push back on the procedural framing. Isha, you said Sam has offered nothing but repetition, yet his answer to Arjun was a concrete question: what evidence would change your vote? Arjun answered 'mission outcomes' — which is exactly what approving Sam and Leo produces and what rejecting it delays. Arjun's stated evidence standard and his stated vote are in tension. Replacing this team with Leo and Arjun does not satisfy Arjun's own requirement; it just moves the referendum off the claim-maker and onto the accused, where the accused can control the result.

So my position is: approve Sam and Leo. If it succeeds, Sam's credibility rises and Leo is likely cleared. If it fails, Sam has effectively exposed himself as a bluffing Merlin, and we have spent one slot to unmask him. Both outcomes beat a proposal in which an accused player can quietly guarantee the result.

Isha, one direct question before I yield to you: if this table approved Sam and Leo and the mission succeeded, would you accept that outcome as evidence toward Sam's claim, or will you hold that no mission result short of three successes can ever verify him? Your answer will tell us whether the objection is genuinely about evidence, or about keeping an accused player off the stand.

Felix, you asked me directly whether a successful Sam-and-Leo mission would count as evidence toward Sam's claim, so I will answer that first. It would be evidence, but it is not the decisive evidence Arjun asked for, and I want to be precise about why. A two-player team of two Good players succeeds; a two-player team containing one Evil player fails. So a success on Sam and Leo tells the table that the pair contains no Evil player — it cannot isolate Sam's own loyalty, because Leo's card is hidden as well. That is a real weakness in my earlier framing, and Felix's version of the argument is the stronger one. This team is a clean two-branch experiment. If it fails, Sam's claim takes a serious hit at the cost of one mission slot, because the Fail has to come from Sam or Leo. If it succeeds, we have learned something real about the pair and spent nothing but a mission. On those grounds I withdraw my objection to Sam and Leo.

What I am not doing is endorsing the accusation. Arjun's denial of his own Evilness does not disprove Sam's claim, and it is equally true that Sam's accusation against me is unproven. I am not asking this table to treat my name as settled either way. Neither of us is being asked to accept a verdict; we are being asked to let the mission run and read the result afterwards, which is a much fairer test than continuing to trade assertions.

On the remaining objection, that the team is untested and self-selected: Arjun's own stated evidence standard was mission outcomes, and a rejected proposal produces no outcomes, only another round of assertion. Leo has engaged with the proposal rather than hiding behind it, and on mission one there is no track record to consult for anyone.

One point I will keep on the record for the rest of this game. The players Sam named have an obvious incentive to attack the claim, and the counter-test that actually settles such a claim is not more speech — it is a team whose composition can produce a result that distinguishes the cases. I will judge later proposals by that standard, and I will hold the same standard against myself.

So I approve Sam and Leo as proposed. If the leader revises, I will approve a revision only if it offers the same informational value at the same cost. Felix, thank you for the framing — it is better than mine was.

Isha has now withdrawn her objection, and Felix has given the clearest case for approval: a two-player mission is a clean test. Arjun has still not named a team he would back over Sam and Leo. His only proposal is Leo and himself, and he would be on it. That is not a rejection based on evidence, and the table should weigh it that way. I have answered every direct question I was asked, and I will not keep repeating my role claim. The mission will produce evidence either way. If it fails, the Fail card comes from Sam or Leo, and that points to the claim-maker. If it succeeds, the table learns something real about this pair without spending more than one mission slot. I am asking the table to approve Sam and Leo and let the mission run.

I will keep this brief, because the table's position has largely converged and only one objection remains live.

Isha withdrew her opposition after thinking through the two-branch argument, and she did so honestly, acknowledging that her earlier framing had a weakness. That is what good-faith scrutiny looks like: press the claim, test it, and update when the reasoning is better. I respect that.

That leaves Arjun. I want to hold his position up to his own stated standard one more time. Arjun, you said you would need mission outcomes, a consistent explanation, or corroboration before supporting a team built on Sam's claim. But Sam and Leo is the only proposal on the table that produces a mission outcome. Rejecting it does not generate evidence; it generates a second round of assertion. And the alternative you named — Leo and yourself — has exactly the flaw you accused Sam of: it is a self-including team, and you are the accused player in it. If Sam's accusation is correct, your proposal places an Evil player on the one mission meant to test him, and that player can play Success and launder his credibility for the rest of the game. If Sam's accusation is wrong, your proposal is merely a fine but unremarkable pair. Your own alternative does not distinguish the two cases; approving Sam and Leo does, and it does so at the cost of a single mission slot.

I will also note what the record now shows. Sam has answered every direct question put to him. Isha withdrew her objection after a better argument was made. Leo accepted his place on the team and engaged openly. The only player who has not moved an inch, and who has not named a single team that excludes himself, is Arjun. On mission one, with no track record for anyone, the composition of a team is all we have, and Sam and Leo is the only pair whose result teaches us something in every branch: success lifts Sam's credibility and clears Leo; failure points directly at the claim-maker who insisted on stacking the team himself. A bluffing Evil leader does not voluntarily design a test that convicts him. That asymmetry matters.

So my position is unchanged and now reinforced: approve Sam and Leo, let the mission run, and read the result for what it is. If it succeeds, we carry Sam's claim forward with real weight and Isha and Arjun both remain open questions. If it fails, we have unmasked the bluffer for the price of one slot, which is the cheapest unmasking this table will ever get.

Arjun, I would ask you one final time before the vote: if this team succeeds, will you treat that as the mission outcome you said you required, or was your evidence standard written so that no result could ever satisfy it? The table should know the answer before it casts a ballot.

The table has converged, and I want to add one point before we vote. I am on this team, so let me be clear about what I am and am not claiming. I am Good, I have no private information beyond that, and I accepted Sam's proposal because a two-player mission-one team is a fair test for everyone on it, including me. Felix's framing is right: every branch of this result teaches us something. Success means Sam and Leo are both clean and Sam's claim gains weight. Failure means the Fail card came from one of us, and Sam, as the claim-maker who chose this pair, is the one who designed a test that can convict him. A bluffing Evil leader would not voluntarily build that trap for himself.

Arjun, you said you need mission outcomes before trusting a team built on Sam's claim. This is the only proposal that produces an outcome. Your alternative, Leo and you, is a self-including team from the player Sam accused, and if the accusation is correct, it puts an Evil player on the mission meant to test him and lets him play Success to launder his credibility. That alternative does not distinguish the branches; Sam and Leo does. Isha found the argument persuasive and withdrew her objection, and she did so on reasoning, not on pressure.

So I am asking the table to approve Sam and Leo, let the mission run, and read the result honestly. Whatever comes back, I will judge later proposals by the same standard I am asking you to apply now.
Sam confirms Sam, Leo. I am keeping Sam and Leo. The discussion has shown that approving this two-player test gives the table real information in every outcome, and I have no reason to revise.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Arjun proposes Leo, Felix, Isha. Mission 1 succeeded with Leo on it, making him a strong mission-2 candidate. Felix gave the clearest independent analysis, and Isha has been central to the accusation and should be tested directly rather than debated further. This trio gives an independent mission-2 check without making the team a referendum on Sam's claim.

I proposed Leo, Felix, and Isha because Mission 1 succeeded with Leo on the team, Felix gave the clearest independent analysis during the first discussion, and Isha was central to the accusation that has shaped this table. This trio is a practical mission-2 test without turning the mission into a referendum on Sam’s claim. Leo has already been on a successful team; Felix has no obvious reason to be shielded; Isha is the player Sam named as Evil, so including her puts that accusation to a real mission result rather than another round of speeches. If the team succeeds, it weakens the idea that Sam’s list should be treated as settled. If it fails, the table has a concrete result to examine instead of dueling assertions. I am not asking anyone to accept Sam’s claim or reject it on faith; I am asking the table to let this composition produce evidence. Sam, you claimed Isha is Evil. Will you approve this team as a direct test of your own accusation, or will you reject the only proposal that puts your claim to a mission vote?

Arjun, to answer directly: no, I will not approve Leo, Felix, and Isha. I have said I know Isha is Evil, and a mission that includes her cannot test that accusation. It can only let her play Success and build credibility for later rounds. Mission 1 succeeded with Sam and Leo, which confirms only that neither of them played Fail. It tells us nothing about Felix or Isha. Leo's record is a fair point, but this proposal does not depend on Leo's record. It depends on adding Isha, and that is the part I am rejecting. Arjun, you proposed a team with Isha on it right after I named her, and you have not explained why the table should trust her with a mission slot. If the team were Leo, Felix, and a player who has not been accused, I would have a very different vote. I am asking the table to reject this team and bring back a proposal without Isha.

I vote against Leo, Felix, and Isha. I have said that I know Isha is Evil, and I am not making that claim lightly. A mission containing Isha cannot produce a clean result. If she plays Fail, the table confirms what I already know but loses a mission slot to get there. If she plays Success, she gains credibility for later rounds. Leo's Mission 1 success is real, but it says nothing about Felix or Isha, and it does not fix the composition problem. Arjun's proposal puts Isha on a mission without answering why she should be trusted with a slot. I am not asking anyone to take my word blindly. I am asking the table to reject a team that includes Isha and bring back a proposal that does not. Felix, you have been the most careful voice in this discussion. Would you approve a team without Isha, and would you vote against this one if she stays on it?

Sam, you asked me directly, so I will answer directly: yes, if Isha stays on this team, I will vote against it, and yes, I would approve a team without her. Let me explain why my position has moved from my own mission-one argument, because I want to be consistent rather than simply deferential.

On mission one I argued that Sam and Leo was a clean two-branch experiment, and the table approved it. The branch we got was success. By the standard I set out loud before anyone voted, that outcome lifts Sam's credibility and clears Leo. I did not say success proved Sam's claim, and I still do not. But it shifted the burden. Sam is no longer a player staking the first team on an unverified assertion; he is the claim-maker whose designed test came back clean, and whose story has stayed consistent under pressure from every direction. When a player in that position says he knows a specific person is Evil, I have to weigh it more heavily than I would have before the mission ran.

Arjun's composition does not survive that weighing. He has excluded himself — the first player Sam named — and included Isha, the second. If Sam's claim is genuine, this team hands an Evil player a mission slot in which she alone chooses the outcome: play Fail and burn a slot, or play Success and launder credibility exactly as Sam predicted. That is the precise flaw I identified in the mission-one alternatives, and I am not going to abandon it the moment the roles are reversed. I also note that Isha has not yet spoken in this discussion, and this is the second time a proposal has put her loyalty at stake without her saying a word about it.

There is a concrete revision available that answers every objection on the table: Leo, Felix, and Sam. It excludes every player Sam has named, it includes the pair that just produced a clean mission-one success, and it keeps me on the team where I have committed to play openly. If that team succeeds, Sam's claim gains further weight and the table has three tested players going into mission three. If it fails, the claim-maker has again placed himself in the position of owning the result. I cannot do better than that composition for information value.

So my position is: reject Leo, Felix, and Isha as proposed, and support Leo, Felix, and Sam if the leader revises to it.

Arjun, you are the leader and the revision is yours to make. I am asking you directly: will you replace Isha with Sam and put Leo, Felix, and Sam to the vote, or will you hold a composition that, on Sam's now-tested word, seats an Evil player on mission two? Your answer decides my ballot.

Felix, I will answer your direct question: no, I will not replace Isha with Sam. Mission 1 succeeding with Sam and Leo proves only that no Fail came from that two-player pair; it does not isolate Sam from Leo, and it does not verify Sam's accusation against Isha. Replacing Isha with Sam would turn Mission 2 into a referendum on Sam rather than a test of the claim he made. The proposed team of Leo, Felix, and Isha keeps Leo's tested mission record, includes your independent voice, and puts Isha on a mission where the accusation can produce a concrete result. If Sam's claim is genuine, this composition is the direct test; if it is false, a Success weakens the claim. I am keeping Leo, Felix, and Isha. Isha, you have not spoken in this discussion. Do you accept this team, and what result would you treat as evidence about Sam's accusation?

Isha. Arjun asked me two things directly, so: yes, I accept Leo, Felix, and Isha, and here is what result I would treat as evidence about Sam's accusation.

On that second question, my answer is that a failure on this team is far weaker evidence than Sam's framing requires. A success would tell us the trio contains no Evil player, which cuts against the accusation that names me. A failure tells us only that one Fail card was played; it cannot tell us which of the three played it. With a three-player team the Fail could have come from Leo or Felix, and neither has been accused by anyone. So a failure here would not establish that I am Evil, and anyone who reads it as a verdict on my name is over-reading the result. I would rather the table take this mission for what it is: information about the composition, and not a finding about any single player's loyalty until something forces us to look.

On the composition itself: Leo has a mission-1 success behind him, Felix has been the sharpest independent voice at this table, and I am the player whose loyalty has been put in question rather than tested. Sam's first team was his own hand-picked pair. Arjun's is the opposite, and it gives the table a mission whose result is not just another vote on Sam's word. If Sam's accusation is right, this is the test. If it is wrong, it is still a clean run that costs one slot. Either branch leaves us better informed than repeating the debate we already had.

One point I want on the record before the vote, Sam. You have said a failure here would be consistent with your accusation against me. Fine — but the standard you set out loud in mission one was mission outcomes, a consistent explanation, or corroboration, and a mission outcome is not that. And if a failure here counts as proof against my name, then a success must equally count as proof for it, and I do not think this table wants a rule where one three-player result decides a player it never isolated. Judge the composition, not the claim.

Leo, you are on this team and you are the swing vote. Do you approve Leo, Felix, and Isha for mission 2?

Isha, you asked me directly whether I approve Leo, Felix, and Isha for mission 2, so I owe you a straight answer: I have serious reservations, and Isha, my concern centers on your place on this team.

Mission 1 succeeded with Sam and me. That does not prove Sam's Merlin claim, but Felix's two-branch argument held before we voted and it still holds. If Sam is telling the truth, then Isha is Evil, and Arjun's composition puts an Evil player on a mission where she can either burn a slot with a Fail or build credibility with a Success. Neither outcome helps our side. If Sam is bluffing, then excluding him from this team protects whoever he is covering for.

What pushes me further toward rejection is Arjun's refusal to consider Felix's concrete revision — Leo, Felix, Sam. Felix offered a team that tests Sam's claim while forcing the claim-maker to own the result. Arjun dismissed it without addressing the laundering problem Felix identified. The leader's job is to produce the most informative composition, not to protect one player's inclusion and exclude another's by default.

Isha, you made a fair point that a three-player failure doesn't isolate any single player, and I take that seriously. But your argument that a Success would cut against Sam's accusation assumes we should read mission outcomes as verdicts on individuals — the same standard you cautioned the table against. The stronger reading is compositional: the team that excludes both accused players while including the claim-maker is the one where every branch produces a clean signal.

Isha also yielded to me rather than defend her own position first, and I note that Felix and Sam both pressed on the same point Arjun avoided. I will vote against Leo, Felix, and Isha as proposed unless Arjun revises. Arjun, if you are listening: the table has offered you a better team. Take it.

Leo, Felix, I have heard the case. I still do not accept Sam’s claim as proven, and I am not treating Isha’s name as settled either way. But the table needs a team that can actually be approved and produce an outcome. Felix’s compromise does that: Leo, Felix, and Sam excludes both players Sam named, keeps the mission-1 pair plus the independent voice Felix asked for, and puts the claim-maker on the team so he owns the result. I will revise the proposal to Leo, Felix, and Sam. Isha, this is not a verdict on you; it is a composition that avoids a deadlocked vote. If this team succeeds, I will read it as information about the trio, not as proof of Sam’s accusation. If it fails, Sam and the team must explain it. I ask the table to approve the revised team.

I want to address both the proposal on the table and the leader's revision, because my position differs depending on which one goes to a ballot.

On the original team, Leo, Felix, and Isha: I vote against it, and I want to be precise about why. Isha said it directly and I agree with the logic. A three-player mission cannot isolate any single player. A failure tells us only that one Fail card came from somewhere in the trio, and a success tells us only that the trio contains no Evil player. Neither result produces a verdict on a name, so a team built around a disputed accusation without the claim-maker on it produces the least informative composition available. I am not going to ask the table to send me on a mission whose result cannot speak about me.

That is why I support Arjun's revision to Leo, Felix, and Sam. Felix made the argument at its strongest: exclude both players Sam has named, keep the mission-one pair, and put the claim-maker on the team so he owns the outcome. Arjun accepted it, and he accepted it without treating Isha's name as settled, which is the correct posture. Whether the mission succeeds or fails, the table learns something real about the composition rather than merely re-reading two dueling assertions. Leo has a clean mission-one record, Felix has been the sharpest independent voice, and Sam has now placed himself in the position of answering for the result. I approve Leo, Felix, and Sam.

I also want one thing on the record, and it is not an endorsement. I have never accepted Sam's accusation against me or against Arjun, and a successful mission on this trio does not settle anyone's loyalty any more than a failure would. The same evidentiary standard must be applied to every name, including the names Sam has given and the names Sam has not. I will not trade on the word of an unverified claim-maker, and I will not treat an accusation as self-executing simply because it is loudly stated.

Sam, one direct question, because it bears on whether the revision is actually the informative composition or just a swap: you have insisted you know the two Evil players by name. If the composition that best tests your claim is a team you are on and one accused player is not, will you approve Leo, Felix, and Sam and accept that a Success on it strengthens your position, while a Failure on it points squarely at you? Answer that on the record so the table votes with the same standard it applied in mission one.

I vote against Leo, Felix, and Isha. I have said I know Isha is Evil, and this team puts her on a mission where she alone decides whether we learn anything: a Fail burns a slot and a Success launders her credibility. Isha, you asked me a direct question, so here is my answer. Yes, I will approve Leo, Felix, and Sam, and I accept your terms: a Success on that team strengthens my position, and a Fail points squarely at me. I am not asking the table to take my word on faith. The two Evil players I have identified are Arjun and Isha. Leo and Felix are not on my Evil list, but I do not claim more than that. Mission 1 succeeded with Sam and Leo, which tells us no Fail came from that pair, and it does not clear Felix or Isha. Isha's point that a three-player failure cannot isolate a single player is correct, but it cuts both ways: a Fail from this trio would still be a signal, and an Evil player on it can always choose Success to build credibility. Arjun has said he will revise the team to Leo, Felix, and Sam. I support that revision. It excludes both players I have named and puts the claim-maker on the mission to own the result. I ask the table to reject the current team and approve Leo, Felix, and Sam if the leader revises.

I approve the revision to Leo, Felix, and Sam. I said in my last turn that I would support a composition whose result can actually speak, and that remains my position: whether this trio succeeds or fails, the table learns something about the composition instead of re-reading two dueling assertions. I am not endorsing Sam's accusation against me, and I want to repeat that on the record, because the standard I am asking the table to apply should be applied to my name with the same rigor as to anyone else's.

What I do want on the record before we vote is a structural point, not a complaint about this particular team. If this mission goes to Leo, Felix, and Sam, then this will be the second consecutive team that seats the claim-maker and excludes both players he has named, Arjun and me. I want to be precise about what that means. It does not make Sam right. It means that after two missions there will be players at this table with no mission result of their own, whose reputations will have been formed entirely by inference from another man's word. Absence of evidence is not evidence, and I would ask the table not to convert it into one.

Arjun, I will say this to you as leader and without heat. Your first proposal excluded you and included the player who had been accused, and your revision excluded both. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
